The **MY** component was designed to model adult mosquito ecology and infection dynamics. 

This vignette takes a deep dive into the design and structure of the **MY** component. It is useful for anyone who wants to learn more about how the code works.  


## Overview 

The **MY** component includes processes related to adult mosquito ecology and infection dynamics. **M** describes the adult mosquito population, and **Y** denotes state variables for pathogen infection dynamics within that population. The state variables and equations depend on the model.

The **Y** component interacts with **X** through blood feeding and transmission: 

+ Infection models use net infectiousness, or $\kappa,$ the probability that a mosquito becomes infected after blood feeding on a human.

+ Each module supplies `F_fqZ`, which computes the daily density of infectious mosquito bites on humans in each patch. The transmission interface uses this quantity to compute EIR for the human strata.

+ Modules also supply `F_fqM`, the daily density of mosquito bites on humans in each patch. The transmission interface uses it to compute HBR for the human strata.

The **M** component interacts with **L** through egg laying and emergence. 

+ The **M** component is developed around the net emergence rate of adult mosquitoes, or $\Lambda.$

+ Each module supplies `F_eggs`, which computes the number of eggs produced by adult mosquitoes in each patch. The egg-laying interface apportions those eggs among the habitats in a patch.

+ `dMYdt` computes derivatives for continuous-time models. Discrete-time models can instead implement `Update_MYt` to update the state variables.

For mosquito ecology, adult mosquitoes emerge from aquatic habitats in the **L** Component and lay eggs into those habitats.*](MY_component.drawio.png)

Two important issues for **MY** components are adult mosquito demography, including mortality and dispersal and the method for handling mosquito bionomics as a baseline that is modified by control.

### Mosquito Demography 

The SI module represents mosquito mortality and dispersal with the matrix $\Omega$ and computes survival and dispersal through the EIP with $\Upsilon = e^{-\Omega \tau}$.

For SI, the matrix is
$$\Omega = \operatorname{diag}(g + \sigma\mu) - K\operatorname{diag}(\sigma(1-\mu)),$$
where $g$ is the mortality rate, $\sigma$ is the emigration rate, $\mu$ is the fraction lost during emigration, and $K$ describes dispersal. Other model families may use different demographic structures.

### Mosquito Bionomics 

Mosquito bionomics must accommodate baseline parameters that can vary with time or environmental conditions and can be modified by vector control. The `MBionomics` and `MEffectSizes` methods update these values for adult mosquitoes. The broader design is described in the [Bionomics vignette](https://dd-harp.github.io/ramp.xds/articles/Bionomics.html){target="_blank"}.

## Required Functions 

There is no fixed number of functions that every **MY** module must implement. The methods required depend on whether the model is continuous-time or discrete-time and on the capabilities the module supports.

Some of these required functions are `S3` class functions in [adult-MY-interface.R](https://github.com/dd-harp/ramp.xds/blob/main/R/adult-MY-interface.R){target="_blank"}. Others are defined for each module. 

One good example is the `SI` module, posted in the `ramp.xds` github repository [adult-MY-SI.R](https://github.com/dd-harp/ramp.xds/blob/main/R/adult-MY-SI.R){target="_blank"}. 

The methods cover model setup, dynamics, bionomics, state variables and initial values, parameter access, parsed outputs, and consistency checks. A module can also implement optional methods such as steady-state calculations when those are supported.

Each module is identified by a class name, generically called `MYname` (for example, `SI`). Most methods dispatch on the class of `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]`, where `s` is the vector-species index. The setup generic instead dispatches on the supplied module name; the skill-set generic accepts either a model or a module name. MY method signatures use `s` consistently.

### Dynamics 

At least one of the following is required, depending on whether the model family is a system of differential equations or a discrete time system:

+ `dMYdt.MYname` :: implement this method for a continuous-time model. It receives `t`, the dependent-variable vector `y`, `xds_obj`, and `s`; it returns derivatives in the same order as the model's state variables. The function is used with solvers such as `deSolve::ode` or `deSolve::dede`.

+ `Update_MYt.MYname` :: implement this method for a discrete-time model. It receives `t`, `y`, `xds_obj`, and `s`, and returns the updated state variables in the model's state-variable order.

### State-variable extraction

`get_MY_vars.MYname` retrieves named state values from the dependent-variable vector $y$.

State-variable getters primarily serve solver evaluations that need
variables by name; users rarely call them directly. Follow the shared
[getter conventions](XH-interface.html#state-variable-getters): describe
extraction from `y`, put index storage in `@note`, and return a named list
of state variables and module-specific derived quantities. Document
GeM's `U` matrix and RMdts's `Y` cohort matrix explicitly.

### Bionomics

Two methods update bionomic parameter values before the dynamics are computed.

+ `MBionomics.MYname` -- evaluates the baseline bionomic parameter functions for the current time and resets the effect sizes to 1.

For every parameter `x` configured as a port, `MBionomics` stores the
baseline in `x_t` and resets `es_x` to 1. `MEffectSizes` then sets
`x = x_t * es_x`. Parameters without ports are stored directly as `x`
and are not modified by effect sizes. This includes EIP and the standard
dispersal-matrix port: use `eip_t`/`es_eip` and
`K_matrix_t`/`es_K_matrix`. Matrix multiplication by an effect size here
is elementwise (`*`), not `%*%`; effects must preserve the dispersal-matrix
constraints. Recompute demographic and survival matrices from the realized
parameters after applying effect sizes. Dynamical parameter accessors such as
`get_f` read the realized values rather than applying effects again;
`get_MY_pars` retains each module's documented parameter-reporting convention.

+ `MEffectSizes.MYname` -- applies vector control effect sizes to the bionomic parameters set by `MBionomics`.

Both methods receive `t`, `y`, `xds_obj`, and `s`, and return the updated `xds_obj`.


### Dynamical Terms 

These methods compute quantities used by other component interfaces. Each returns a vector with one value per patch.

+ `F_fqZ.MYname` - returns the daily density of infectious mosquito bites on humans in each patch. The transmission interface uses it to compute EIR by human stratum.

+ `F_fqM.MYname` - returns the daily density of mosquito bites on humans in each patch. The transmission interface uses it to compute HBR by human stratum.

For biting-output documentation, use "Compute infective mosquito biting density
for `module` (**MY**)" for `F_fqZ` and "Compute mosquito biting density for
`module` (**MY**)" for `F_fqM`; generic titles omit "for `module`".
Describe daily biting density on humans for each patch, not a per-host biting
rate. Return documentation is "a [numeric] vector of length `nPatches`".
Link each method to its counterpart and document dispatch on
`xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]` in the generic notes.

Preserve model-specific formulas: basicM returns zero infective biting;
SI obtains infective density using `Upsilon %*% Y`; BQ, BQm, and BRQS use
the blood-feeding states only. Flag implementation discrepancies rather than
silently changing them: the three behavioral-state modules currently obtain
`q` using `get_f`. `F_fqZ.SI` converts its matrix-product result to a numeric
vector, preserving one value per patch.

+ `F_eggs.MYname` - returns daily egg production by adult mosquitoes in each patch. The egg-laying interface distributes the eggs among habitats.

Use "Compute egg production for `module` (**MY**)" for method titles and
"Compute egg production (**MY**)" for the generic. Use the description
"Return the number of eggs laid by the adult mosquito population, per patch"
and return "a [numeric] vector of length `nPatches`".
Methods inherit the module NULL anchor's `Egg Laying` section using
`@inheritSection module Egg Laying`. In that section, explain the egg-laying
population and formula: total adult density `M` for basicM, GeM, macdonald,
RMdts, SI, and SEI; gravid density `Qu+Qy+Qz` for BQ, BQm, and BRQS.
Multiply that density by `nu` and eggs per batch (`eggs_per_batch` in GeM,
`eggsPerBatch` in the other modules). Link methods to their module and
`EggLaying`; document dispatch on `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]` in the generic note.

### Dynamical parameter accessors

`get_f`, `get_q`, `get_g`, and `get_sigma` return the stored realized feeding
rate, human blood fraction, adult mosquito mortality rate, and patch emigration
rate, respectively. They do not evaluate ports or apply effect sizes.
Refresh port-backed values through bionomics and effect-size application first.
These accessors differ from `get_MY_pars`, whose parameter-reporting convention
is documented by each module.

Use "Get the parameter for `module` (**MY**)" with the parameter's full name
in method titles; generic titles omit "for `module`". Use a short description
identifying the stored realized parameter per patch, inherit the module NULL
anchor's `Parameters` section, and return "a [numeric] vector of length
`nPatches`". Put dispatch on `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]` in the generic note.
For BQ, BQm, and BRQS, `get_sigma` returns `sigma_b`, the blood-feeding
emigration rate, not `sigma_q`. Their `get_g` methods read the generic `g`;
BRQS's mismatch with its state-specific mortality parameters remains deferred.
The trivialMY mortality and emigration accessors return empty numeric vectors.

### Mosquito-matrix accessors

`get_Omega(xds_obj, s = 1)` returns the stored mosquito demographic matrix,
$\Omega$, and `get_Upsilon(xds_obj, s = 1)` returns the stored EIP
survival-and-dispersal matrix, $\Upsilon$, for the selected species.
These shared functions read `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]$Omega` and
`xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]$Upsilon`, respectively; they do not recompute matrices
or modify the model object. Each returns a matrix of dimensions `nPatches`
by `nPatches`, or `NULL` if the corresponding matrix is not stored.

Use the titles "Get the mosquito demographic matrix (**MY**)" and
"Get the EIP survival-and-dispersal matrix (**MY**)". Keep storage paths
and the distinction between retrieval and recomputation in `@note`.
Link the getters to each other, their corresponding `change_Omega` or
`change_Upsilon` function, and `xds_info_mosquito_demography`.
Do not implement module-specific getter methods.

### MY Model Object

Each module defines a constructor and setup method for its **MY** model object. The constructor returns a list with the module's class; the setup method stores it at `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]` and prepares its initial values and shared interfaces.

+ `make_MY_obj_MYname` :: returns the module-specific **MY** object. It typically contains:

    + bionomic parameter values or bionomic parameter objects. In most models, the value of baseline bionomic parameters are functions of time, or exogenous variables that vary with time.  
   
    + `class(MY_obj)` = `MYname` 
    
    + the indices for the model variables, stored as `MY_obj$ix`
    
    + the initial values are stored as `MY_obj$inits` 
    
    + anything else that is needed can be configured here 
    
+ `setup_MY_obj.MYname` calls the constructor and stores the object for vector species `s` at `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]`. It also prepares initial values and any shared interfaces needed by the module.

### Parameters

+ `get_MY_pars.MYname` returns the module's parameters as a named list.

+ `change_MY_pars.MYname` changes supported parameter values after setup. New values are passed by name in `options`.

### Initial Values

A set of functions sets up or changes the initial values for the state variables.

+ `make_MY_inits_MYname` - returns a named list of default initial values for all state variables. Values can be overridden through `options`.
    
+ `setup_MY_inits.MYname` - calls the initial-value constructor and stores the values at `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]$inits`.

+ `get_MY_inits` and `change_MY_inits.MYname` - inspect and change the stored initial values.

`get_MY_inits` is an ordinary function, not an S3 generic. It returns the
selected species' stored `inits` field directly: a named list of initial
values, an empty list if stored, or `NULL` if absent (as in `trivialMY`).
Keep storage in a documentation note and link to setup/change functions;
follow the shared getter wording in the
[documentation conventions](XH-interface.html#initial-value-constructors).

Title the constructor "Make initial values for `module` (**MY**)" and
describe it as "Create a named list of initial values for the `module`
module. Values in `options` override the defaults." Its return description
is "a named [list] of initial values". Preserve model-specific explanations.
Document numeric scalar expansion to `nPatches`, except that `RMdts` uses
`nPatches * max_eip` for `Y`. State the `SI` restriction `Y < P < M`.
Describe accessory initialization: `GeM` initializes `U` from `Upsilon`
and `d1`, `d2`, and `d3` to zero; `macdonald` initializes `dk_ix` to zero.
These accessory values are not independently set through `options`.
The constructor, setup method, and change method each link to the other
two in `@seealso`, following the shared
[documentation conventions](XH-interface.html#initial-value-constructors).

Use "Set up initial values for `module` (**MY**)" as the setup-method title.
Describe calling the initial-value constructor and `options` overrides.
Put the actual storage location in `@note`, and return "an **`xds`** model
object". Preserve special cases: GeM computes an EIP matrix for its
constructor.

Title initial-value changers "Change initial values for `module` (**MY**)".
Use "Change initial values named in `options` for the `module` module,
leaving other values unchanged." Describe supported values and special
behavior, put storage explanations in `@note`, and return "an **`xds`**
model object". Keep reciprocal constructor/setup links. Flag implementation
discrepancies separately rather than treating this contract as validation.

Read unspecified values from the selected module's `inits` list. RMdts
rebuilds that list with its initial-value constructor and the selected
species' `max_eip`, so its `Y` values have length `nPatches * max_eip`;
scalar overrides are expanded by the constructor.

### Initial-density accessors

`get_M` and `get_Z` return initial adult and infective mosquito densities,
respectively, not current solver states or output trajectories. Use
"Get the initial adult mosquito density for `module` (**MY**)" and
"Get the initial infective mosquito density for `module` (**MY**)" for
method titles; generic titles omit "for `module`". Descriptions are
"Return the initial adult mosquito density per patch." and
"Return the initial infective mosquito density per patch."

Methods inherit the module NULL anchor's `State Variables` section and link
to the module and `get_MY_inits`. Keep SI's infective-density explanation in
its inherited anchor section rather than repeating the derivation.
Return "a [numeric] vector of length `nPatches`"; generic notes describe
dispatch on `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]`.
The implemented methods are `get_M` for basicM, GeM, macdonald, RMdts,
and SI, and `get_Z` for GeM, macdonald, RMdts, and SI.

### Variable indices

`setup_MY_ix.MYname` sets up indices for the model's state variables.
`get_MY_ix` retrieves the stored indices.

`get_MY_ix(xds_obj, s = 1)` is an ordinary function defaulting to vector
species 1, not an S3 generic. It returns the module's stored `ix`
field directly: a named list of variable indices, an empty list if stored,
or `NULL` if absent. Document storage in `@note`, link to `setup_MY_ix`,
and follow the shared [index-getter conventions](XH-interface.html#variable-index-setup).

Use the title "Set up variable indices for `module` (**MY**)".
Describe consecutive allocation after `xds_obj$max_ix`, list the actual
block order and lengths, and return "an **`xds`** model object".
Put index storage and the updated maximum in `@note`, following the shared
[indexing conventions](XH-interface.html#variable-index-setup).
Most blocks have length `nPatches`; GeM's `U_ix` has length `nPatches^2`,
and RMdts's `Y_ix` has length `nPatches * max_eip`.

Store indices at `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]$ix`, including for RMdts and BRQS.
State extraction, output parsing, and dynamical terms must use this same
module-level location. Index setup returns the updated model object.

### Standard Outputs

`get_MY_orbits(xds_obj, s = 1)` retrieves saved, parsed orbits (trajectories) after
solving for **MY** for the selected species. It returns a list of module-specific
outputs with `time` added from `xds_obj$outputs$time`. It reads
`xds_obj$outputs$orbits$MY[[s]]`; it does not parse outputs or modify the model.
Use the title "Get orbits (**MY**)" and the shared
[orbit-getter conventions](XH-interface.html#output-parsers).

Follow the shared [output-parser conventions](XH-interface.html#output-parsers):
use "Parse outputs for `module` (**MY**)", describe extraction from `outputs`
into a named list, and use "a [list]" for returns. Document index storage at
`xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]$ix` and any derived quantities, including differences
between `parous` and `parity`, cohort aggregation, and omitted auxiliary states.
Parsers return results; the output-processing pipeline stores them at
`xds_obj$outputs$orbits$MY[[s]]`. They do not update the model object themselves.
The RMdts parser sums cohorts within each patch at each output time.

`parse_MY_orbits.MYname` parses the model's state variables and any model-specific derived quantities from the solver output. During output processing, `ramp.xds` also records `fqZ`, `fqM`, egg production `G`, emergence `Lambda`, and net infectiousness `kappa`. The transmission interface uses `fqZ` and `fqM` with the biting-distribution matrix to compute EIR and HBR, respectively.

### Consistency Checks

The skill set describes a module's capabilities and compatibilities. The consistency-check interface provides a place to implement model-specific checks before solving.

Non-trivial modules report `<parameter>_is_port` for `f`, `q`, `g`,
`sigma`, `sigma_b`, `sigma_q`, `mu`, `nu`, `eip`, and `K_matrix`.
Each flag is `TRUE` for a parameter implemented as a port and `FALSE` for
a direct or absent parameter. These flags describe the current module
implementation, not whether a port's current value varies with time.

+ `check_MY.MYname` :: provides a hook for model-specific checks before solving. Existing methods currently return the model unchanged and perform no checks.

+ `get_skillset_MY.MYname` :: returns the module's capabilities and compatibilities as a list. A module without `Update_MYt.MYname` must include `dts = FALSE`.

## Optional Functions 

Optional methods should be implemented only when they are meaningful for the model. Record supported capabilities and compatibilities in the skill set.

### Steady States

The interface provides optional methods for steady states under static parameter values.

+ `steady_state_M.MYname` :: pass the emergence rate of adult mosquitoes and compute steady states for the **M** component. 

+ `steady_state_MY.MYname` :: pass the emergence rate of adult mosquitoes and net infectiousness, and compute the steady states for the **MY** component.

+ `steady_state_Y.MYname` :: pass adult mosquito population density and net infectiousness, and compute the steady states for the **Y** component.

Follow the shared steady-state documentation conventions in the XH interface:
identify inputs, supported equation systems, actual return types, and state
names. Method titles use "Compute steady states for `module` (**MY**)".
The three generics dispatch on `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]`. The Y generic requires
a module-specific method; it does not provide a default calculation.

`steady_state_M.basicM` delegates to `steady_state_M_basicM`, which dispatches
on `xds_obj$xds` to select `xde` or `dts`. Both return a numeric vector with
the `M` block followed by the `P` block. `steady_state_MY.SI` similarly
delegates to `steady_state_MY_SI`, but only its `xde` method is implemented;
it returns a list with `M`, `P`, and `Y`. GeM and macdonald return lists
with `M`, `P`, `Y`, and `Z`. These functions return values without storing
them on the model object. The SEI calculation currently references undefined
`M_eq` and requires repair before use.

### Visualization

The MY interface does not define MY-specific plotting generics. A module may provide model-specific visualization functions that use its parsed outputs.

The shared helpers `xds_plot_M`, `xds_plot_Y`, and `xds_plot_Z` plot saved
adult, infected, and infective mosquito densities, respectively.
`xds_plot_Y_fracs` and `xds_plot_Z_fracs` plot the saved fractions
`y = Y/M` and `z = Z/M`; they do not calculate those fractions.
All read the required fields and `time` through `get_MY_orbits` for the
selected species and draw one line per patch. The parsed outputs must
contain the requested quantity.

Plot helpers create a new plot unless `add = TRUE`. Their corresponding
`xds_lines_*` helpers require an existing plot. A single `clrs` or `llty`
value applies to all patches; vectors supply one value per patch.
All helpers return `invisible(NULL)`.
Use titles such as "Plot infected mosquito density (**MY**)" and
"Add lines for the infected mosquito fraction (**MY**)", distinguishing
infected `Y` from infective `Z`. Put required fields and plot/overlay
behavior in `@note`, document colors and line types by patch, and link each
plot helper to its corresponding line helper.

## Documentation conventions

Follow the shared [function order](XH-interface.html#function-order) in module
and component files and in guide implementation sections. Keep functions with
their documentation and preserve file-level review/TODO notes at the top.

Follow the shared [documentation conventions](XH-interface.html#documentation-conventions)
for titles, equations, descriptions, notes, return values, and punctuation.
Use **MY** as the component tag. For example, a derivative method title is
"Compute the derivatives for `module` (**MY**)", while an update method
title is "Update states for `module` (**MY**)".

The method description must show the equations it actually computes,
including accessory states and delay-dependent branches when present.
For derivative methods, begin "Compute the derivatives for the `module` module:"
and retain the equations immediately below. Inherit the module's state,
parameter, dynamical-term, and ODE or Dynamics sections as appropriate.
Use "a [numeric] vector of derivatives in the module's state-variable order"
for returns. Document returned block order in `@note`, including matrix
flattening and accessory derivatives where applicable. The generic documents
dispatch on `xds_obj$MY_obj[[s]]`. The trivialMY method retains its empty-vector
description and return value.

Update method titles use "Update states for `module` (**MY**)".
Begin descriptions "Update the state variables for the `module` module:"
and show the updating equations in `\deqn{}` immediately below.
Inherit the same NULL-anchor sections as the derivative method, using `DTS`
instead of `ODE`. For the current update methods, these are `State Variables`,
`Dynamical Terms`, `Parameters`, and `DTS`; SEI's update inherits `DTS`
rather than its continuous-time `Dynamics` section. RMdts has no derivative
method and follows the same four-section pattern.
Document actual returns: basicM and SI return numeric vectors, while RMdts
returns a list of `M`, `P`, `U`, `Y`, and `Z` and SEI returns a list of `M`
and `Z`. Their interface discrepancies remain TODOs, not runtime changes.

Keep storage and dispatch mechanics in `@note`, rather than using them as
the functional description.

Constructors use "Make a module object for `module` (**MY**)" as their
title. Describe parameter initialization and `options` overrides, and
identify the parameter getter and changer. The constructor,
`get_MY_pars.MYname`, and `change_MY_pars.MYname` each link to the other two
in `@seealso`. Document separately managed parameters, such as dispersal
matrices, without implying that the changer updates every getter output.

Parameter-changer titles use "Change parameters for `module` (**MY**)".
Start the description with "Change parameter values named in `options`
for the `module` module, leaving other values unchanged." Retain static-port
restrictions, separate dispersal-setup instructions, and any bionomics or
matrix refresh performed by that method. After parameter or port changes,
call `MBionomics(0, y, xds_obj, s)` using the flattened initial state `y`;
do not call `MEffectSizes` from the changer. Return an **`xds`** model object.

### Setup documentation

Use the title "Set up the module object for `module` (**MY**)" and start
the description with "Set up a/an `module` module object for the **MY**
component and the \(s^{th}\) vector species." In roxygen, write the species
index as `\eqn{s^{th}}`.

List the actual setup actions in code order: module-name assignment when
present, construction using `nPatches` and `options`, skill-set setup,
initial values, and the shared interfaces used by that module. Initial
values may occur before or after interface setup; follow the implementation.
End with "Return the updated **`xds`** model object."

Use these phrases for the corresponding interface steps:

- "Initialize the circadian function using `[setup_F_circadian.setup]`."
- "Initialize the mosquito demographic matrix port."
- "Initialize the EIP survival and dispersal matrix port." Include this
  step for methods that configure the active EIP port; omit it from the
  `basicM` and `SEI` setup descriptions.
- "Initialize the mosquito dispersal matrix using `[setup_K_matrix.zero]`."
  For behavioral-state models, use "matrices" and retain the `which_K`
  choices (`Kb`, `Kq`, and, for `BRQS`, `Ks`).

In roxygen, the bracketed helper names above are links; in `ramp.library`,
qualify them with `ramp.xds::`. These phrases describe initialization, not
a promise that setup computes every matrix. The computation of Omega and
Upsilon is outside this documentation convention.

See [Developing MY Modules](https://dd-harp.github.io/ramp.library/articles/MY-How_To_Add_Model.html)
for an adaptable template.
